scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Flame and the Apostles: The Sacred Circle of Margamkali
This is Margamkali. 17th century.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Margamkali is an ancient round dance of the Saint Thomas Christian community in Kerala, primarily maintained by the endogamous Knanaya (Southist) sub-ethnic group.
Its origins are linked by scholars to Malabar Jewish diaspora dance patterns as well as Kerala Brahmin performance arts such as Sangam Kali and Yathra Kali.
The word 'Margam' signifies the path to salvation, and historically 'Margam Koodal' referred to Christian conversion.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Margamkali is danced during Christian community celebrations, church feasts, weddings, and state cultural showcases.

It serves as a visual and oral devotional recreation of the 3rd-century apocryphal Acts of Thomas, detailing his arrival on the Malabar Coast, his miracles, his trials, and the establishing of crosses and churches.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in a circular formation around a lit brass lamp (Nilavilakku).

Typically executed by a dozen dancers, the performance consists of two main parts (padham): a narrative singing and clapping phase recounting Saint Thomas's life, followed by Parichamuttukali, a martial phase incorporating artificial swords and shields.
Dancers synchronize rhythmic stepping and hand-clapping to the timekeeping of palm-sized cymbals played by the singer.
Watch for Nilavilakku step, Parichamuttukali segment.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Margamkali features no musical instruments other than two small, palm-sized cymbals played by the main singer.

The vocal text consists of 14 stanzas (padas) composed in a style related to Tamil Cindu literature, incorporating Syriac liturgical vocabulary such as maran (our Lord), alaha (God), mar thomma (St Thomas), malaka (angel), and Iso (Jesus).
Listen for the palm-sized cymbals.

A lead vocal narrative chanting 14 stanzas in Middle Tamil and Syriac devotional terms, punctuated solely by the metallic rhythmic strike of a pair of small, palm-sized cymbals without external drums or melodic instruments.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers traditionally wear the Chattayum Mundum, the traditional attire of Saint Thomas Christian women of Kerala.
The setting centers on a lit Nilavilakku (oil lamp) placed on the floor; the flame represents Christ and the surrounding dancers represent his twelve disciples.
Originally performed by men and boys, it is now widely danced by women and school students.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Significant figures in the tradition include Anjilimootil Itti Thomman Kathanar (17th-century priest and lyricist), Kalarikal Unni ashan, Indumoottil Kocheppu ashan, Indumoottil Kutto ashan, compiler Puttanpurikkal Uthuppu Lukose (1910), Dr. Chummar Choondal (folk culture scholar), Fr.
George Karukaparambil, Jacob Vellian, and Bishop Mar Kuriakose Kunnasserry.
Historically, distinct Northist (Saint Thomas Christian) and Southist (Knanaya) versions existed.
The art form was preserved orally across generations through village masters called ashans.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Margamkali is a sacred Christian devotional art form centered on a lit lamp representing Christ. Outsiders should respect the sacred nature of the performance, lyrics, and symbolisms.
